16248:
In the Sumerian love songs, the shepherd Dumuzi courts and marries the goddess Inanna. In the *Descent of Inanna*, Inanna returns from the underworld needing a substitute and, finding Dumuzi sitting on a throne instead of grieving for her, hands him over to the demons. In *Dumuzi's Dream* he flees and is caught. A fragment published by Samuel Noah Kramer in 1963 suggests that Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna divide the year, each spending half in the underworld.

The death of Dumuzi was lamented in ritual songs, and the fourth month of the Babylonian calendar (June-July) bore his name. Older scholarship (James Frazer's *The Golden Bough*) made him the model 'dying and rising god' of fertility; modern specialists stress that Dumuzi's return is barely described and that the 'dying and rising' category was over-generalised. Debated.
16249:
In a vision dated 592 BC, Ezekiel is taken to the temple and shown a series of 'abominations', each worse than the last. At the north gate he sees 'women weeping for Tammuz' (Ezek 8:14) — a public mourning rite for a foreign god held at Yahweh's house. Then, worse still, twenty-five men turn their backs to the temple to worship the sun (Ezek 8:16). The vision explains why the glory of God departs (Ezek 10:18-19).

Two other passages are sometimes linked to Tammuz or his western counterpart Adonis, but both links are debated: the 'pleasant plants' and 'strange slips' of Isa 17:10-11 (possibly the quick-sprouting 'gardens of Adonis'), and 'the desire of women' disregarded by the king of the north in Dan 11:37, which some read as Tammuz/Adonis and others as the hope of the Messiah or simply natural affection.
16250: Ezekiel's vision exposes a mourning rite for Ishtar's lover held at the north gate of the temple, part of a sequence of increasingly serious violations.
16252: Isaiah describes plantings that sprout quickly and then fail. Some scholars see the 'gardens of Adonis', small pots of fast-growing seeds used in mourning for the dying god. Debated.
16254: The arrogant king ignores 'the desire of women'. One reading takes this as Tammuz/Adonis, a god popular among women; others reject the link.
16258: Tablets of the Descent of Inanna, Dumuzi's Dream and love songs show the myth behind the mourning rite. Kramer's 1963 publication of the ending revised earlier views of the story.
16261: The Akkadian version ends with instructions for the rites of Dumuzi, including lamentation, which corresponds to what Ezekiel saw.
16262: The fourth month of the Jewish calendar is still called Tammuz, a name adopted from Babylonian usage during the exile. Jerome wrote that a grove of Tammuz-Adonis had been planted over the cave of Jesus' birth at Bethlehem (Jerome, *Letter* 58.3), which some historians accept and others treat cautiously. Syriac and Arabic writers mention Harranian women still mourning 'Ta'uz' in the Middle Ages. Milton includes 'Thammuz' among the fallen angels.

16274: Hathor (and Sekhmet) as the Eye of Ra
16279: Ra was Egypt's sun god, believed to sail across the sky by day and through the underworld by night. Pharaohs called themselves 'son of Ra'. Joseph married the daughter of a priest of Ra's great city, On, and many readers see the plague of darkness as a blow aimed at Ra — a traditional reading that scholars debate.
16280: At Heliopolis the creator Atum (merged with Ra as Atum-Ra) rose on the first mound out of the waters of chaos and produced the other gods. Each day Ra crossed the sky in his 'day-boat'; each night he travelled through the twelve hours of the underworld in his 'night-boat', where the chaos-serpent Apophis tried to swallow him and had to be defeated so the sun could rise. In the *Destruction of Mankind* story, Ra, grown old, sends his Eye (as Hathor-Sekhmet) to punish rebellious humans and then has to trick her with red-dyed beer to stop the slaughter.
16281:
Ra is never named in the Hebrew Bible, but he is present in names and places.

- Joseph married Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Gen 41:45; Gen 41:50; Gen 46:20). Potiphera means 'the one whom Ra has given'. On is Heliopolis, the sun-god's city.
- The store-city Rameses (Exod 1:11) bears the name of Pharaoh Ramesses ('Ra has fashioned him').
- Jeremiah predicts that Nebuchadnezzar will 'break the pillars of Beth-shemesh' (house of the sun) in Egypt (Jer 43:13) — the obelisks of Heliopolis. Ezekiel mocks On by spelling it Aven, 'wickedness' (Ezek 30:17).

**The plagues.** God says the Passover judgement is 'against all the gods of Egypt' (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4). Many interpreters therefore read the ninth plague — three days of darkness that could be felt, while Israel had light (Exod 10:21-23) — as a direct humiliation of Ra. This pairing is traditional and widely taught, but the text itself does not name Ra, and Egyptian gods had overlapping roles, so scholars disagree on how far to press one-plague-one-god charts. Treat it as a reasonable but debated reading.
16282: Joseph marries into the priesthood of On
16283: Pharaoh gives Joseph an Egyptian name and Asenath, daughter of the priest of the sun-city. The narrative notes this without comment; later Jewish writers (the romance *Joseph and Aseneth*) felt the need to tell of her conversion.
16284: Darkness over Egypt (traditional link to Ra; debated)
16285: Three days of darkness fall on Egypt while the Israelites have light. Because Ra was the supreme sun god and Pharaoh his son, many read this as the clearest plague-against-a-god. The Bible's explicit claim is broader: judgement on 'all the gods of Egypt'.
16286: Breaking the obelisks of the sun-city
16287: Jeremiah, taken to Egypt against his will, predicts Babylon will shatter the sacred pillars of Heliopolis. Ezekiel renames On as Aven, 'trouble/wickedness'.
16289: Israel is forbidden to bow to the sun. Josiah removes horses and chariots dedicated to the sun; Ezekiel sees men in the temple bowing eastward to the sun.
16291: standing since c. 1950 BC; site excavated repeatedly since the 19th century
16293: The only obelisk still standing at Heliopolis, from the sun temple of Ra. Other Heliopolis obelisks were carried off in antiquity, including the pair now called Cleopatra's Needles in London and New York.
16296: Large fragments of a royal statue found in the Heliopolis sun-temple area, first reported as Ramesses II and then identified as Psamtik I (7th century BC), showing royal investment in Ra's city during the period of Judah's late kings.
16297: Aven ('wickedness') in Ezek 30:17; Beth-shemesh ('house of the sun') in Jer 43:13
16298: Ezekiel changes the vowels of On to make 'Aven', the same word Hosea used to mock Bethel as Beth-aven, 'house of wickedness' (Hos 4:15). Jeremiah translates the city's meaning into Hebrew.
16299: Ra remained central throughout Egyptian history, merging with Amun and later identified by Greeks with Helios. Heliopolis declined after Alexandria was founded, and its stones were used to build medieval Cairo. Ra's name survives in pharaohs' names such as Ramesses and in the modern popularity of Egyptian sun imagery.
16311: kingship passed from father to son
16313: A mummified king with green or black skin, holding the crook and flail and wearing the white atef crown; the djed pillar (his backbone)
16324: Osiris was Egypt's god of the dead: a murdered king who was brought back to life to rule the underworld and judge souls. Every dead Egyptian hoped to become 'an Osiris'. The Bible never mentions him, but Egypt's death culture forms the background to Joseph's embalming, and some scholars connect Pharaoh's 'heavy heart' with Osiris's judgement scale.
16325:
Osiris was a good king of Egypt. His jealous brother Seth killed him (in later versions, by trapping him in a chest and later cutting his body into pieces scattered across Egypt). Osiris's wife Isis searched for him, gathered and wrapped his body — the first mummy — and conceived their son Horus by the revived Osiris. Osiris then became king of the underworld, while Horus grew up to defeat Seth and take the throne of the living. Each living pharaoh was identified with Horus, and each dead pharaoh with Osiris.

In the *Book of the Dead* (New Kingdom, from about 1550 BC), the dead person's heart is weighed on a scale against the feather of Maat (truth) in the presence of Osiris. A heart heavy with wrongdoing is eaten by the monster Ammit; a light heart passes on to eternal life.
16326:
Osiris is not named in Scripture.

- **Embalming.** Joseph orders Egyptian physicians to embalm Jacob, which takes forty days, with seventy days of mourning (Gen 50:2-3), and Joseph himself is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt (Gen 50:26). The text records this without endorsing Egyptian afterlife beliefs; Joseph asks that his bones be carried to Canaan (Gen 50:25; Exod 13:19).
- **Pharaoh's heavy heart.** Exodus often says Pharaoh's heart was 'heavy' (Hebrew *kabed*, Exod 7:14; Exod 8:15; Exod 9:7). Some Egyptologists and biblical scholars (for example John Currid) suggest an ironic allusion to the weighing of the heart: Pharaoh's heart is heavy, so he fails the very judgement Osiris was supposed to preside over. Others think *kabed* simply means stubborn. Debated.
- **Plagues.** Exod 12:12 announces judgement on 'all the gods of Egypt'. Popular charts link Osiris to the first plague (the Nile was sometimes called his outflow) or to the death of the firstborn (as lord of the dead). These pairings are traditional and debated; the text names no individual god.
16328: Israel's patriarchs receive Egyptian burial practices, yet Joseph's dying wish looks beyond Egypt to the promised land.
16329: The heavy heart of Pharaoh (possible Osiris allusion; debated)
16330: The repeated language of a 'heavy' heart may play on Egyptian judgement imagery, ironically marking Pharaoh as condemned.
16331: Judgement on all the gods of Egypt
16332: The death of the firstborn, including Pharaoh's heir (the living Horus), is presented as God's verdict on Egypt's divine order. Any specific Osiris link is interpretive.
16334: 1903 (identified by Margaret Murray under Flinders Petrie); cleared 1912-1914 (Naville)
16335: Abydos, behind the temple of Seti I
16336: A sunken, island-like cenotaph representing the tomb of Osiris surrounded by water, built under Seti I (c. 1290 BC).
16339: A Middle Kingdom official describes organising the annual Osiris festival, a procession re-enacting the god's death and restoration — one of the oldest descriptions of religious drama.
16340: Papyrus of Ani (Book of the Dead)
16343: Beautifully painted scenes of the weighing of the heart before Osiris, the best-known illustration of Egyptian judgement after death.
16344: Under the Ptolemies, Osiris was fused with the Apis bull as Serapis, a Greek-looking god promoted to unite Greeks and Egyptians. Isis and Osiris-Serapis cults spread across the Roman Empire and competed with early Christianity. Some popular writers claim the Gospels copied the Osiris myth; most historians reject this, noting that Osiris is not raised to bodily life on earth but becomes king of the dead.
16348: Father of the gods (title in Nile hymns)
16353: A plump man with a pot belly and drooping breasts, crowned with papyrus or lotus plants, carrying offering tables of food
16354: First Cataract region, Elephantine/Aswan (believed source of the flood); also Gebel el-Silsila
16355: Hapi was the god of the Nile's yearly flood, which fertilised Egypt's fields and made the country rich. He was not 'the river' itself so much as the life-giving inundation. The first plague, turning the Nile to blood, is traditionally read as a blow against Hapi and the Nile's sacred status — a link the text implies only in general terms.
16356: Hapi had almost no myths; he was praised rather than narrated. The Middle Kingdom *Hymn to the Nile* (Hymn to Hapi) thanks him for bringing food, making the barley and emmer grow, and filling the granaries, and warns that if he is slow, people starve. He was imagined as living in a cave near the First Cataract at Aswan, pouring the flood from jars. Hapi should not be confused with Apis (Egyptian Hep), the sacred bull.
16357:
Egypt's dependence on the Nile flood is a theme across the Bible. Moses tells Israel that the promised land is 'not as the land of Egypt', watered by foot-powered irrigation, but a land that 'drinks water of the rain of heaven' (Deut 11:10-11) — a land dependent on God rather than on a river.

**First plague.** Moses strikes the Nile, its water turns to blood, the fish die and the Egyptians cannot drink (Exod 7:14-25). Because the Nile and its flood were divine gifts embodied in Hapi (and associated with Osiris), the plague is widely read as an attack on Egypt's source of life and on its gods. The pairing is traditional and plausible, but the text names no Egyptian god, so it should be presented as interpretation (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4).

Ezekiel later calls Pharaoh 'the great dragon that lies in the midst of his rivers, which has said, My river is my own, and I have made it' (Ezek 29:3) — the claim to own and create the Nile is what God condemns. Isaiah's oracle on Egypt predicts the Nile drying up and fishermen mourning (Isa 19:5-8).
16358: The Nile turned to blood (traditional link to Hapi; debated)
16359: The first plague strikes the river on which all Egyptian life depended. Interpreters link it to Hapi, Osiris or the Nile's divine status in general.
16361: Israel's new land will depend on rain from God, not on a predictable river — a theological contrast with Egypt's flood-god.
16362: Pharaoh claims to have made the Nile
16363: The prophets judge Egypt's boast that the river belongs to Pharaoh, predicting its failure.
16364: Hymn to the Nile (Hymn to Hapi)
16365: copies in papyri acquired in the 19th century (e.g. Papyrus Sallier II, Anastasi VII)
16367: A Middle Kingdom hymn praising the flood as the giver of all food. It shows how completely Egypt's life was tied to the Nile — the background to the first plague.
16371: A Ptolemaic-era inscription telling of seven years of low Nile floods and famine under the ancient king Djoser, ended by honouring the god Khnum of the cataract. It is often compared with Joseph's seven years of famine (Gen 41:25-36), though it is much later and legendary.
16373: in use from antiquity; studied since the 19th century
16375: A staircase gauge used to measure the height of the flood, on which taxes depended.
16376: Hapi continued to be depicted on temple walls into Roman times. The Nile flood stopped being annual after the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.
16383: A frog, or a woman with a frog's head
16384: Her-wer, Middle Egypt (approximate; exact site not securely located)
16385: Khnum, the ram-headed potter god who shaped bodies on his wheel
16386: Heqet was an Egyptian goddess shown as a frog, who helped women in childbirth and was linked with the breath of new life. Frogs swarmed from the Nile each year after the flood, so they symbolised abundance. The plague of frogs is often read as a mockery of Heqet, but this is a traditional, debated link.
16387: Heqet had few stories. In some traditions she gave the breath of life to the bodies her husband Khnum shaped on his potter's wheel. In the Westcar Papyrus story of the birth of three kings, Heqet is one of the goddesses who come disguised as midwives and 'hasten the birth'. Women wore frog amulets and used ivory birthing wands decorated with frogs and other protective figures. Because frogs appeared in huge numbers after the flood, the frog also became a hieroglyph for the number 100,000.
16388:
Heqet is not named in the Bible.

**Second plague.** At Moses' word, frogs come up from the Nile and fill houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens and kneading bowls (Exod 8:1-15). When they die they are piled in heaps and the land stinks. Pharaoh's magicians can produce more frogs but cannot remove them, and Pharaoh has to ask Moses to pray. Many interpreters see a deliberate mockery of a goddess of fertility and life: the symbol of blessing becomes a smothering nuisance and then a stinking ruin. This is a traditional reading; the text itself makes no mention of Heqet, and frogs were associated with other deities too. Treat as debated.

There is also a possible irony that some readers point out: the Egyptian goddess of midwives is overshadowed by the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who fear God and preserve Israel's babies (Exod 1:15-21). This link is speculative.

In Revelation, unclean spirits 'like frogs' come out of the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet (Rev 16:13) — perhaps an echo of the Exodus plague.
16389: Frogs over the land (traditional link to Heqet; debated)
16390: A creature associated with fertility and blessing becomes a plague. Pharaoh is made to ask that the frogs be removed 'that you may know there is none like the LORD our God' (Exod 8:10).
16392: Revelation's frog-like demonic spirits gather kings for battle, probably drawing on the Exodus plague imagery.
16393: Ivory apotropaic 'birth wands' and frog amulets
16394: excavated at many sites since the 19th century
16395: Middle Kingdom tombs and towns across Egypt
16396: Curved ivory wands carved with protective beings including frogs, used to protect mothers and newborns, show Heqet's role in everyday religion.
16400: A collection of tales including the birth of three kings attended by Isis, Nephthys, Meskhenet and Heqet disguised as midwives.
16401: Frog amulets remained popular in Egypt into the Roman era, and early Egyptian Christians used frog-shaped lamps, some with inscriptions such as 'I am the resurrection', reinterpreting the frog as a symbol of new life.
16404: Hapi (not to be confused with the Nile god)
16408: the living 'herald' of the god Ptah

16410: Memphis (temple of Ptah); burials at the Serapeum, Saqqara
16414: Apis was a real, living bull kept at Memphis and worshipped as the earthly form of the god Ptah. When an Apis bull died it was mummified and buried in a giant stone coffin, and priests searched Egypt for its successor. Some scholars see Apis behind the golden calf, and the Greek Bible explicitly names Apis in Jeremiah.
16415: Apis was chosen by markings: a black bull with a white triangle on the forehead, a vulture- or eagle-shaped patch on the back and other signs. Its mother was said to have been impregnated by a flash of light from heaven. The bull lived in a special enclosure at Memphis, gave oracles by its movements, and appeared in festivals. On death it became one with Osiris (Osiris-Apis), and in the Ptolemaic period this fused god became Serapis, worshipped across the Mediterranean.
16416:
Apis is not named in the Hebrew Bible, but there are three points of contact.

1. **The fifth plague.** A severe pestilence kills Egypt's livestock, including cattle, while Israel's animals are spared (Exod 9:1-7). In a culture that venerated sacred bulls and cows, this is often read as judgement on Apis and the cow goddess Hathor. Traditional; the text names no god (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4). Debated.

2. **The golden calf.** Some interpreters think Israel, fresh from Egypt, modelled the calf (Exod 32:4) on Apis. Others point out that a young bull was also the standard Levantine symbol for El and Baal, and that Aaron proclaimed a 'feast to the LORD' (Exod 32:5), suggesting an image of Yahweh or a pedestal for him rather than an Egyptian god. Debated; see golden-calf.

3. **Jeremiah 46:15 in Greek.** The Hebrew reads 'Why are your mighty ones (or: your mighty one) swept away?' The Septuagint divides the Hebrew letters differently and translates, 'Why has Apis fled? Your chosen calf did not stand.' Most scholars think the Greek translators preserved a genuine reference to Apis, which the later Hebrew text obscured.
16417: Cattle struck by pestilence (traditional link to Apis and Hathor; debated)
16418: Egypt's livestock die while Israel's survive, a blow often read as aimed at Egypt's sacred cattle.
16420: In the Greek translation, Jeremiah's oracle on Egypt mocks the flight of the Apis bull before Nebuchadnezzar.
16422: Stephen says that the Israelites 'turned back in their hearts to Egypt' and made a calf. Whether the calf imitated Apis is debated.
16426: Long underground galleries hold twenty-four enormous granite and basalt sarcophagi, most from the Late Period. Inscribed Apis stelae dating the bulls' births and deaths have helped Egyptologists fix the reigns of pharaohs.
16430: Herodotus (*Histories* 3.27-29) claims the Persian king Cambyses stabbed the Apis bull. A Serapeum epitaph shows an Apis buried with royal honours under Cambyses, so many historians doubt Herodotus's story.
16433: The decree of Ptolemy V praises the king for generous gifts to the Apis and Mnevis bulls, showing the sacred bulls' importance into the second century BC.
16435: The same consonants can be divided into different words. The Greek translators read a mention of Apis (Hep). Many scholars think this was the original sense.
16436: Through Serapis, the Apis cult outlived pharaonic Egypt. The Serapeum of Alexandria became one of the great temples of the Roman world until its destruction in AD 391 under the bishop Theophilus — a turning point in the end of paganism in Egypt.
16447: A cow, or a woman with cow ears or horns holding a sun disc; the sistrum (a sacred rattle)
16450: Hathor was a much-loved Egyptian goddess of love, music, motherhood and joy, often shown as a cow. She was also the 'Lady of Turquoise' at the Egyptian mines in Sinai. Some interpreters connect her with the golden calf and with the plague on Egypt's cattle; both links are debated.
16451: Hathor was the 'Eye of Ra'. In the *Destruction of Mankind*, Ra sends her out to punish rebellious humans; she becomes the raging lioness Sekhmet and begins to slaughter them. To stop her, Ra floods the fields with beer dyed red to look like blood; she drinks it, becomes drunk and gentle, and returns as loving Hathor. Festivals of drunkenness re-enacted this. As the celestial cow she was also pictured as the sky itself and as the nurse of the king.
